client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away three months ago. Things I used to love, like going for walks or cooking a nice meal, just feel completely pointless now. I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying right now — this deep grief and the loss of meaning in things you once loved — makes complete sense given what you've been through. It takes a lot of courage to try something even when part of you doubts it will help, and that small act of reaching out matters more than you might realize right now. I'd love to understand more about your experience — when you say those activities feel pointless, what kinds of thoughts tend to go through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, when I try to do something I used to enjoy, like reading or going for a walk, my mind just kind of goes blank and then fills up with this thought like "what's the point of any of this." It's like there's this voice that reminds me that no matter what I do, I still come home to an empty apartment and nobody really notices whether I did anything or not. I guess I feel invisible, and that makes everything feel kind of hollow.
therapist: That feeling of invisibility — like your actions don't register with anyone in the world — sounds quietly devastating, and it makes so much sense that it drains the color out of things you used to enjoy. That thought, "what's the point," is doing a lot of heavy work in those moments, and I'd gently want to explore it with you — because while it feels very true right now, grief has a way of making that voice sound more certain than it actually is. When that thought shows up, do you notice it arriving as an absolute fact, or is there ever even a tiny flicker of doubt about whether it's completely true?

client: I mean... I guess if I'm being really honest, there's maybe a small part of me that isn't completely sure it's true all the time. Like, there are rare moments where I think maybe someone does notice me, but then it feels so fragile and fleeting that it almost makes it worse, you know? It's like catching a glimpse of something and then having it disappear, which just reinforces the "what's the point" feeling even more.
therapist: That glimpse you're describing — that small, honest part of you that isn't completely sure — is actually really significant, even if it feels fragile and painful right now. It's interesting that when those moments of connection or being noticed appear, the grief almost amplifies them into something that hurts more, as if your mind is using them as evidence *for* the "what's the point" story rather than against it. I'm curious — can you tell me about one of those rare moments where you felt someone did notice you, and what that was actually like before the doubt rushed in?

client: There was this one time at work, maybe a few months ago, where a colleague stopped me in the hallway and said she'd noticed I always seemed really thoughtful in meetings, that I asked questions other people didn't think to ask. For maybe thirty seconds I felt this warmth, like I actually existed to someone, you know? But then almost immediately I started thinking she was just being polite, or maybe she wanted something from me, and the whole thing curdled into this anxious mess.
therapist: That moment in the hallway sounds genuinely beautiful — thirty seconds of really feeling seen for something real about you, your thoughtfulness, the way your mind works — and it's so telling that your first instinct was to protect yourself by finding a reason it couldn't be true. That pattern, where something warm arrives and your mind immediately works to dismantle it, is really common in grief, but it's worth noticing that it's a habit of thought rather than a fact — your colleague's words were real, whatever her reasons. I wonder, if you tried to just sit with that memory for a moment right now, without the "but maybe she was just being polite" part — what does it feel like to let it be true, even just as an experiment?

client: It's... actually kind of hard to do that, just let it sit there without picking it apart. When I try, there's this brief moment where it feels warm, like maybe I do matter to someone at work, but then almost immediately I feel guilty, like I'm being arrogant or self-congratulatory for believing it. I guess I've spent so long feeling invisible since my friend moved away that I don't really trust those moments anymore.
therapist: It's such a tender and important thing you just noticed — that accepting someone's kindness feels dangerous, like it might mean something unflattering about you, rather than simply being something you deserve. That guilt rushing in to shut down the warmth isn't humility, it's actually another way your mind has learned to keep you safe from disappointment, especially after losing so much connection — your partner, your friend moving away. I'm curious, where do you think that equation came from — that believing you matter to someone equals arrogance — is that a message that feels familiar from earlier in your life?

client: Yeah, it does feel familiar, actually. I think growing up, any time I seemed too confident or like I thought I was special, it got shut down pretty fast — like I was being a brat or full of myself. So I guess I learned early that thinking you matter to people is something you're supposed to keep quiet about, or it'll get taken away from you.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — as a child you learned that feeling like you matter is something fragile and dangerous, something that invites punishment or loss, and so you built a very understandable rule to protect yourself: stay small, stay invisible. The painful irony is that the very shield that kept you safe back then is now the thing that makes it so hard to let in the warmth that's genuinely there for you — from your colleague, from others who notice you. I'm wondering, now that you can see that old rule a little more clearly, does it feel like it still makes sense to follow it as an adult, or does part of you feel ready to gently question it?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually does recognize that pattern — like, intellectually it makes sense. But when you ask if I'm ready to question it, there's this immediate tightness in my chest, almost like a warning signal going off that says "don't you dare." It's hard to explain, but questioning that rule feels less like freedom and more like standing on the edge of something I could fall off of.
therapist: That tightness in your chest, that "don't you dare" — that's not resistance or you being stuck, that's actually the old protective part of you doing exactly what it learned to do, and it deserves some real respect before we ask it to step aside. You don't have to leap off that edge — in fact, real change in CBT rarely looks like a leap, it looks more like just leaning forward slightly and noticing you didn't fall. I'm wondering, what would feel like the tiniest, safest possible step — not abandoning that rule entirely, but just... loosening it a little, in one small moment?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually appreciates that framing — like, it's not me being broken, it's just this old system trying to keep me safe. But when I try to think of what that "tiny step" would even look like, my mind just goes blank, because the rule feels so all-or-nothing — either I keep everyone at arm's length or I completely fall apart and become this needy, overwhelming person nobody wants around. I guess the tiniest thing I can imagine is maybe... not immediately changing the subject when someone asks how I'm doing, but even just thinking about that makes my stomach clench.
therapist: That "tiny step" you just named — pausing instead of deflecting when someone asks how you're doing — is actually not tiny at all, it's quietly courageous, and the fact that your mind found it on its own matters. I also want to gently notice that all-or-nothing picture you described, either keeping everyone at arm's length or becoming "too much" — that's the old rule talking, because it doesn't leave any room for the middle ground where most real human connection actually lives. What do you imagine might actually happen in that middle space, if you let someone's "how are you" land for just a moment — not a full unburdening, just a breath of honesty?

client: I hear what you're saying about the middle ground, and part of me wants to believe that exists, but honestly it's hard to picture without it feeling kind of... fake? Like if I pause and give a little honest answer, I'm worried it'll come across as performative, or the other person will just give me a polite response and move on, and then I'll feel even more alone than if I'd just said "fine." I guess the fear is that the middle ground just ends up being the worst of both worlds.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — you'd be taking a small risk and the anticipated reward feels uncertain, while the pain of a hollow response feels very concrete and guaranteed. But I want to gently point out something: your mind is predicting that outcome with a lot of confidence, almost like it's already decided how the other person will respond, which is actually the old protective rule working hard to make the risk feel not worth taking. I'm curious — has there ever been a moment, even once, where you let a little honesty through with someone and it didn't go the way the fearful part of you predicted?

client: I mean... yeah, there was this one time with my coworker Diane. I told her I was feeling really overwhelmed with the project load, kind of half-expecting her to just brush it off or tell me to push through, but she actually said she felt the same way and we ended up talking for like an hour. But I think I keep forgetting that because it feels like a fluke, like Diane is just unusually kind and most people wouldn't react that way.
therapist: Diane isn't a fluke — she's evidence, and it's really worth sitting with the fact that your honesty with her didn't lead to the worst-case scenario your mind keeps predicting, it led to an hour of genuine connection. It's a very human thing to dismiss the moments that contradict our fears and hold tightly to the ones that confirm them, but you've now named two real examples — Diane, and your colleague who noticed your thoughtfulness — where being seen didn't end in disaster. I'm wondering, what would it mean about you, and about the world, if these moments weren't flukes but were actually small pieces of a truer picture?
